served.stem: A neuron receives a much stronger stimulus than before. How does it signal the greater intensity?
choices: The resting potential becomes more negative
It fires action potentials more frequently
The action potential travels faster down the same axon
served.bankWhy: A light switch is either on or off, so the neuron cannot shout louder with a bigger spike. Instead it shouts more often. Stimulus strength is coded as firing frequency.

answer.text: It fires action potentials more frequently
answer.line: Every action potential is all or none, the same height every time. So a stronger stimulus shows up as more spikes per second.

steps: Know the rule: an action potential is all or none, the same size and shape every time.
So a single neuron cannot signal louder with a bigger spike. It signals more often.
Stronger stimulus, higher firing frequency. The nervous system can also recruit more neurons.

choices.text: The resting potential becomes more negative
choices.note: A stronger stimulus depolarizes the cell. A more negative rest would make it harder to fire, not easier.

choices.text: It fires action potentials more frequently

choices.note: Graded potentials do grow with the input, which is why this pulls. The action potential is the all-or-none exception: always the same height.

choices.text: The action potential travels faster down the same axon
choices.note: Conduction speed comes from axon diameter and myelin, not stimulus strength. A faster signal means a different axon.
A receptor potential lasts as long as the stimulus does. The action potential's duration is fixed by its channels.

student.lockIt: Action potentials never grow. A stronger stimulus means more of them per second.
student.hook: Louder means more often, not bigger.
